title: File Sync and Storage
prompt: Design a service where people keep a folder of files in sync across their laptop, phone and the web, and can share folders with others.

clarify.q: What is the largest file we must support, and what is typical?
clarify.why: Most files are a few MB, but a 50 GB video file rules out whole-file upload and makes block-level transfer and resume mandatory.

clarify.q: Do clients sync a real folder on disk, or is it a web drive only?
clarify.why: A desktop sync client must detect local edits, work offline and reconcile later, which is where conflicts come from. A web-only drive is just upload and download.

clarify.q: Can two people edit the same file in a shared folder?
clarify.why: If yes, concurrent edits are normal, not rare, and we need a defined conflict rule. Real-time co-editing of document contents is a different product (operational transforms or CRDTs).

clarify.q: How long do we keep old versions and deleted files?
clarify.why: Version history keeps old blocks alive, so it decides storage growth and when garbage collection may delete a block.

clarify.q: How fast must a change on one device appear on another?
clarify.why: A few seconds means a push channel (long-poll or WebSocket) to every online device. Minutes would allow polling, which is far cheaper but feels broken to users.

clarify.q: Are files end-to-end encrypted so the server cannot read them?
clarify.why: Client-side encryption makes cross-user deduplication impossible and kills server-side previews and search. It is a product decision with a big storage cost.

clarify.q: Do we need to run on mobile with limited storage?
clarify.why: Mobile usually syncs metadata only and downloads file contents on demand, which changes what 'in sync' means per device.

functional: A change to a file on one device appears on the user's other online devices within 10 s.
Clients work offline and upload their changes when they reconnect.
Uploading an edit to a large file sends only the changed parts, not the whole file.
Concurrent edits to the same file never silently lose data; the losing edit is kept as a conflicted copy.
A user can share a folder with others with view or edit permission.
A user can restore a previous version of a file or a deleted file within 30 days.
nonFunctional: Durability of committed file data: 11 nines. Losing a file is the worst possible bug.
Metadata is strongly consistent within a folder tree: two devices never see the same file at different 'latest' revisions after both have synced.
Metadata API p99 under 200 ms; block transfer limited by the user's bandwidth, not by us.
99.95% availability for sync; downloads of existing files should keep working even if commits are degraded.
Up to 30 M concurrently connected devices.

assumptions: 50 M users, 20 M daily active, ~1.5 devices online per active user at peak
Average 8 GB stored per user in files averaging 2 MB, so ~4 000 files each
Each active user changes 20 files a day and uploads ~10 MB of new bytes a day after block dedupe
Block size averages 4 MB; dedupe and compression save ~25% of logical bytes
Each change must be pushed to ~2 other devices on average

steps.label: Logical and physical storage
steps.math: 50 M × 8 GB = 400 PB logical; × 0.75 after dedupe = 300 PB; × 1.5 erasure coding = 450 PB raw disk

steps.label: Block index size
steps.math: 300 PB / 4 MB = 75 B blocks; × ~80 B per entry (hash, location, refcount)
steps.result: ≈ 6 TB of block index: a sharded KV store, not one DB

steps.label: File metadata size
steps.math: 50 M × 4 000 = 200 B file entries; × ~300 B each
steps.result: ≈ 60 TB of metadata, sharded by namespace

steps.label: Push notifications
steps.math: 400 M changes × 2 devices = 800 M/day ≈ 9 300/s; 30 M open connections / 100 k per server

estimates.takeaway: Bytes and metadata are different problems. File bytes are huge (hundreds of PB) but immutable once written, so a content-addressed blob store with erasure coding is right. Metadata is small per row but needs strict ordering and transactions, and at 60 TB it must be sharded, ideally by something that keeps one folder tree on one shard. The 30 M idle connections cost more servers than the commit rate does. Sending only changed blocks is what keeps ingest at ~20 Gbps instead of several times that.

api.note: Before uploading, ask which blocks the server already has. Often most are already there.

api.body: raw block bytes (up to 4 MB, compressed)
api.note: Content-addressed and idempotent: the server re-hashes and rejects bytes that do not match the name.
Atomic per file. 409 means someone else committed first; 412 means blocks are missing and must be uploaded first.
Ordered journal of changes since the cursor. The client stores the cursor durably.

api.returns: 200 { changed: [nsId...] } after a change or 60 s
api.note: Long-poll (or a WebSocket) that only says 'something changed'. The client then calls /changes.
Turns the folder into its own namespace that both users mount.

entities.name: Namespace
fields: a user's root or a shared folder
entities.why: The unit of ordering and of sharding. Everything inside a namespace lives on one shard, so commits are single-shard transactions.

entities.name: JournalEntry
entities.why: Append-only history. Clients sync by reading it from their cursor. Version history and restore read old entries.

entities.name: FileLatest
entities.why: Current state per path for fast lookups and the conditional update that detects conflicts.

entities.name: Block
entities.store: Sharded KV (e.g. a Cassandra-style or RocksDB-backed store), key = hash
fields: blob store key or volume id
number of live file versions using it
entities.why: 75 B rows only ever read by exact key, so a KV store fits. Ref counts drive garbage collection.

entities.name: Mount
entities.why: Lets one shared namespace appear in many users' trees without copying it.

data.note: A namespace is the core idea: a user's home folder is one namespace and each shared folder is another. Commit, ordering and conflict detection all happen inside one namespace, which is one shard, so they are plain database transactions. A commit inserts a JournalEntry with seq = latestSeq + 1 and updates FileLatest only WHERE rev = baseRev. The block store is content-addressed (key = sha256(bytes)), so the same bytes are stored once and a block is never modified in place.

hld.summary:
The desktop client watches the sync folder, splits changed files into blocks and hashes them. It talks to two services. The block service stores and serves immutable blocks in a blob store, indexed by hash in the block index. The metadata service owns namespaces, the change journal and conflict detection, backed by a sharded metadata DB.

After every commit the metadata service publishes a small event to a change bus. The notification service holds long-poll or WebSocket connections from every online device and tells subscribed devices that a namespace moved forward. Those devices then pull the journal from their cursor and fetch only the blocks they lack. A GC worker deletes blocks whose reference count has been zero for longer than the retention window.

diagram.title: Metadata path, block path and change notifications
diagram.src:
flowchart LR

  C1 --> BS[Block service]
  BS --> BI[(Block index KV)]
  BS --> BLOB[(Blob store)]
  MS --> MDB[(Metadata DB sharded by namespace)]
  MS --> BUS[[Change bus]]
  BUS --> NS[Notification service]

  C2 --> BS
  GC[Block GC worker] --> BI
  GC --> BLOB

flows.title: Saving an edit to a 100 MB file on the laptop
steps: Client notices the file changed, re-chunks it and hashes each block; 25 blocks, of which 1 is new.
Client calls /blocks/check with 25 hashes; the server says 1 is missing.
Client uploads the 1 missing block (4 MB instead of 100 MB).
Client commits { path, baseRev: 7, blockList } and the server checks rev = 7, writes rev 8 and journal seq 9 001.
Metadata service publishes 'namespace advanced to 9 001' on the change bus.

flows.title: Phone picks up the change
steps: Phone has an open long-poll to the notification service for its namespaces.
Notification service sees the event and returns { changed: [nsId] }.
Phone calls /changes from its cursor 9 000 and receives entry 9 001 with the new block list.
Phone downloads only the blocks it does not have locally, rebuilds the file, then saves cursor 9 001.

flows.title: Two devices edit the same file while offline
steps: Laptop and desktop both start from rev 7 of report.docx.
Laptop reconnects first and commits rev 8.
Desktop commits with baseRev 7; the server returns 409 with currentRev 8.
Desktop renames its local version to 'report (desktop conflicted copy).docx', commits it as a new file, then pulls rev 8 of the original.
Both versions now exist on every device; nothing is lost.

deepDives.title: Block-level chunking and deduplication
deepDives.problem: Uploading whole files on every save is wasteful: a 1 GB file with a 10 KB edit would send 1 GB. Splitting into blocks fixes that, but how we split matters. With fixed-size blocks, inserting one byte near the start shifts every later boundary, so every block hash changes and we re-upload the whole file anyway. We also need to decide how widely to dedupe, because dedupe across users has privacy costs.

options.name: Whole-file upload
options.how: Hash and upload the full file on every change.
cons: Bandwidth scales with file size, not edit size
A failed 5 GB upload restarts from zero
No sharing of identical bytes between versions

options.name: Fixed-size blocks (4 MB)
options.how: Cut at every 4 MB offset; hash each block with SHA-256.
pros: Works well for files edited in place (databases, VM images, many media files)
cons: An insertion shifts all later boundaries, so a 1-byte insert near the start of a 100 MB file re-uploads all 25 blocks

options.name: Content-defined chunking
options.how: Slide a rolling hash over the bytes and cut wherever its low bits hit a target pattern, with min 1 MB, average 4 MB, max 16 MB.
pros: Boundaries follow content, so an insert changes only 1–2 chunks
Better dedupe between versions and between similar files
cons: More client CPU to scan every byte
Variable chunk sizes make the block index and resume logic a bit more complex

deepDives.choice: Content-defined chunking with a ~4 MB average, hashed with SHA-256, and blocks compressed before upload. It is what makes 'send only the changed parts' true for documents and archives where edits insert bytes. Fixed blocks are acceptable for a first version if most files are small (most files here are under one block anyway), so this is a scaling choice, not a day-one must. Dedupe scope: dedupe within an account and its shared namespaces by default. Global, cross-user dedupe saves more, but it leaks information: if an upload of a known file is skipped, an attacker learns someone already stores it. It also cannot coexist with client-side encryption. I would allow global dedupe only with a proof-of-ownership step and never for encrypted accounts.

deepDives.title: Metadata DB versus block store
deepDives.problem: The two kinds of data have opposite shapes. Blocks: hundreds of PB, write-once, read by exact hash, no relations. Metadata: about 60 TB, constantly updated, needs ordering per folder, conditional updates for conflict detection, and listings by path. One store cannot serve both well, and the hard part is keeping them consistent: metadata must never point to a block that is missing, and GC must never delete a block someone still uses.

options.name: Everything in object storage
options.how: Store each file version as an object and keep the folder tree as JSON objects.
cons: No transactions, so conflict detection and ordering are not possible reliably
Listing a folder or 'what changed since X' is slow and expensive

options.name: Metadata in a sharded relational DB, blocks in a blob store
options.how: Relational DB sharded by namespace holds journal and current state; blobs live in an erasure-coded store keyed by hash, with a KV index for ref counts.
pros: Single-shard transactions give atomic commits and compare-and-set
Blob store is cheap per byte and scales without coordination
cons: Two systems must be kept consistent
A very large shared namespace can become a hot shard

options.name: Metadata in a distributed SQL database
options.how: Use a globally distributed SQL store (Spanner-style) for all metadata, blocks still in a blob store.
cons: Higher write latency and cost per commit
Still needs careful key design to avoid hot ranges

deepDives.choice: Sharded relational metadata plus a content-addressed blob store. Keep them consistent with ordering rules, not distributed transactions. Write path: blocks are uploaded and made durable first; commit checks that every hash in the block list exists before it writes the journal row, so metadata never points to a missing block. Delete path: a commit that drops a block from a file's latest version only decrements ref counts asynchronously; GC deletes a block only after it has been unreferenced for longer than the 30-day version window plus a safety margin. A rare orphan block costs a few MB; a wrongly deleted block loses a file, so every rule favours orphans. I would consider distributed SQL if cross-namespace moves (dragging files between shared folders) became common enough that two-shard commits hurt.

deepDives.title: The sync protocol
deepDives.problem: Every device must converge on the same state, even after days offline, with millions of devices connected at once. Pushing full change data to every device is wasteful and fragile. Polling every few seconds from 30 M devices would be ~10 M requests/s of mostly empty answers. The protocol must be resumable, idempotent and cheap when nothing changes.

options.name: Periodic full scan
options.how: Every few minutes the client lists the whole remote tree and diffs it against local state.
cons: Cost grows with tree size, not change size: 4 000 files per user × 20 M users
Changes take minutes to appear

options.name: Server pushes full change records
options.how: On each commit the server sends the full entry over each device's socket.
cons: Missed messages while offline need a separate catch-up path anyway
Server must buffer per device, which is hard at 30 M devices

options.name: Cursor-based journal plus a thin notify channel
options.how: Each namespace has an ordered journal. Devices store a cursor per namespace. A long-poll or WebSocket only says 'namespace X advanced'; the device then pulls /changes from its cursor.
pros: One code path for online and offline catch-up
Idempotent: replaying from an old cursor is safe
Notify messages are tiny and can be dropped without harm
cons: Two round trips for each change
Very old cursors past journal compaction need a full rescan fallback

deepDives.choice: Cursor-based journal with a thin notify channel. It treats 'online' as just 'offline with a very short gap', so there is only one sync algorithm to get right. The notify message can be lost and nothing breaks, because the next notify or a 60 s timeout triggers a /changes call that catches up. The client applies entries in seq order and saves the cursor only after the files are on disk, so a crash replays the last batch safely. For large shared namespaces with many members, notify fan-out goes through the change bus partitioned by nsId. If a cursor is older than the journal's retention, the server returns 'reset' and the client does a full listing once.

diagram.src:

  M-->>L: rev 8 at seq 9001

  P->>M: changes since 9000

  P->>B: download missing blocks

deepDives.title: Conflicts and concurrent edits
deepDives.problem: Two devices can edit the same file without seeing each other's change: one was offline, or both saved within the same second. The server must detect this reliably and the user must never lose work. Folder operations add more cases: one device renames a folder while another adds a file inside it, or one deletes a file the other edited.

options.name: Last writer wins by timestamp
options.how: Whichever commit arrives last, or has the later mtime, becomes the file.
cons: Silently destroys one person's edit
Device clocks are wrong often enough to pick the older version

options.name: Optimistic concurrency with conflicted copies
options.how: Every commit carries the baseRev it was edited from. If the server's current rev differs, reject with 409; the client keeps its version as a sibling 'conflicted copy' file.
pros: Detection is a single conditional update
cons: Users must merge by hand
Conflicted copies pile up if a shared folder is busy

options.name: Automatic content merge
options.how: For known formats (plain text) do a three-way merge of base, ours and theirs.
pros: No manual merge for the easy cases
cons: Only works for a few formats
A bad merge is worse than a visible conflict because nobody notices

deepDives.choice: Optimistic concurrency with conflicted copies, enforced by UPDATE FileLatest SET rev = rev + 1 ... WHERE nsId = ? AND path = ? AND rev = baseRev inside the commit transaction. Track files by fileId so a rename on one device and an edit on another apply cleanly instead of conflicting. For edit-versus-delete, the edit wins and the file is restored, because recreating is safer than losing. For folder renames, the journal records a move of the folder and children follow it. I would add automatic merging only for plain text and only if users ask; real co-editing belongs in a separate collaborative editor product.

failures: A client crashes after uploading blocks but before committing
Blocks are content-addressed and idempotent, so the retry skips them. Unreferenced blocks are collected later by GC after the safety window.

Fail over to a synchronous replica so no acknowledged commit is lost. Clients retry commits; the baseRev check makes retries safe. Downloads of existing blocks continue because the block store is separate.
The notification service loses all connections after a deploy
Devices reconnect with jitter over a few minutes and immediately call /changes from their cursors, so no change is missed. Rate-limit reconnects per server to avoid a stampede.
A GC bug starts deleting live blocks
GC only deletes blocks unreferenced for 30+ days and moves them to a soft-delete bucket for another week. Run a canary that checks random live files can be fully read. Pause GC on any mismatch.
A user's client syncs a folder with 2 M tiny files, flooding one shard
Rate-limit commits per namespace, batch many small commits into one transaction, and move very large namespaces to a dedicated shard.
Bit rot corrupts a stored block
Erasure coding repairs from other fragments. Background scrubbing re-hashes blocks and compares with the stored hash. Clients also verify hashes after download.
scale: 10× users: metadata grows to ~600 TB. Add shards by namespace and move namespaces between shards with a directory service. The block store just adds storage nodes.
Huge shared namespaces (a company folder with 50 k members) become hot shards and fan-out storms. Give them dedicated shards, and batch notifications per namespace every second.
Cold data: most bytes are rarely read after a month. Move blocks not read in 90 days to a cheaper cold tier with higher read latency.
Multi-region: keep each namespace's metadata primary in one home region, replicate blocks to a second region, and serve block downloads from the nearest copy.

followups.q: How does sharing a folder work if each user has their own namespace?
answer: The shared folder becomes its own namespace with its own journal and shard.
Each member gets a Mount row that places it at a path in their tree; the client syncs the mount like any namespace.
Permissions are checked on the namespace, so revoking access is one row change.

followups.q: How do you sync to a phone with 64 GB of storage and a 2 TB account?
answer: Sync metadata (the journal) fully, but download contents on demand when the user opens a file.
Let users pin folders for offline use; those sync contents eagerly.
Evict least-recently-opened contents when storage is low.

followups.q: How do you resume a 50 GB upload?
answer: Block-level upload is resumable for free: /blocks/check tells the client which blocks already arrived.
The client commits only after all blocks are up, so a half-uploaded file is never visible to other devices.

followups.q: Why not let clients write blocks and metadata in one request?
answer: Blocks are large and slow; holding a metadata transaction open during a 4 MB upload would destroy DB throughput.
Separating them keeps metadata transactions in milliseconds and lets block uploads retry freely.

followups.q: How do you stop a ransomware-infected laptop from syncing encrypted garbage everywhere?
answer: Detect a burst of rewrites with high-entropy content across many files and pause sync for that device.
Version history lets the user roll the whole namespace back to a point in time.
Notify the user and require confirmation before resuming.

mistakes: Uploading whole files on every change instead of only changed blocks.
Using fixed-size blocks and claiming it handles inserts efficiently.
Resolving conflicts with last-writer-wins and silently losing edits.
Storing file bytes in the metadata database, or metadata in object storage with no transactions.
Pushing full change payloads over sockets and having no catch-up path for offline devices.

mid: Separated file bytes (blob store) from metadata (database) and said why
Split files into blocks and uploaded only changed blocks
Used a push channel or long-poll so other devices learn about changes within seconds
Asked about sharing, file size limits and version history before designing
Gave a conflict rule that does not lose data
senior: Estimated storage, commit rate and connection count with shown arithmetic
Explained content-defined chunking and why fixed blocks fail on inserts
Designed a cursor-based journal per namespace that handles offline catch-up with the same code path
Detected conflicts with a baseRev compare-and-set inside a single-shard transaction
Ordered writes so metadata never references missing blocks, and GC only deletes long-unreferenced blocks
staff: Discussed the privacy and encryption trade-off of cross-user dedupe
Handled hot shared namespaces and notification fan-out for large teams
Planned safety nets for data loss bugs: soft-delete, scrubbing, read canaries, GC pause
Covered mobile on-demand sync and cold-tier storage as cost levers
